specPoints.text: know how to represent a metallic lattice by a 2-D diagram
understand metallic bonding in terms of electrostatic attractions
explain typical physical properties of metals, including electrical conductivity and malleability

primer.text: From Ionic Bonding you already know that metal atoms lose their outer electrons to form positive ions. This note keeps those electrons instead: in a pure metal the outer electrons are released into a shared sea that flows around an array of positive ions, and that single picture explains conduction, malleability and the high melting points of metals.

lessons.title: Metallic bonding & the lattice diagram
lessons.opening: A metal is a giant structure of atoms arranged in a regular pattern. Within the lattice the atoms release their outer electrons, turning into positive ions, while the released electrons become delocalised and move freely between the ions like a sea. The metallic bond is the strong attraction between those positive ions and the delocalised electrons, and a simple 2-D diagram shows ions in rows with the electrons scattered between them.
keyPoints: A metal is a giant structure whose atoms sit in a regular, repeating pattern.
Within the lattice the atoms lose their outer electrons, becoming positive metal ions.
The released outer electrons are delocalised and move freely between the positive ions.
The metallic bond is the strong pull that the positive ions and the electron sea exert on each other.
A 2-D diagram of the metallic lattice shows rows of ions with delocalised electrons between them.

low.restatement: Picture rows of positive metal ions with small electrons scattered freely between them. Each ion pulls on the shared sea of electrons, and the sea pulls back on every ion at once, which is the metallic bond holding the whole structure together.
low.analogy: Think of marbles set in a fixed grid, all sitting in one shared puddle of glue: every marble touches the same glue, and the glue is what grips the whole tray together.
low.examPointer: In the 2-D diagram, label the ions with their positive charges and show the electrons between the rows; both parts carry credit.

medium.restatement: The lattice forms because metal atoms relinquish their outer-shell electrons, generating an array of positive ions bathed in delocalised electrons. Electrostatic attraction between the ions and the shared electron sea acts throughout the structure, and the same attraction is what the 2-D diagram of rows and free electrons is drawn to represent.
medium.analogy: Picture a tray of ball bearings resting in oil that flows freely between them: the oil reaches every ball at once, and any pull on the oil is felt by the whole tray.
medium.examPointer: Use the full phrase attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons; naming only one party leaves the bonding explanation incomplete.

check.stem: What happens to the outer electrons of the atoms in a metal lattice?

options.text: They are released and become delocalised, moving freely between the positive ions
options.explanation: The outer electrons leave their own atoms and belong to the whole structure, forming the electron sea.

options.text: They transfer to neighbouring non-metal atoms
options.explanation: There are no non-metal atoms in a pure metal; the electrons stay within the lattice.

options.text: They are shared in pairs between two atoms only
options.explanation: Localised shared pairs describe covalent bonding; metallic electrons are shared across the whole lattice.

options.text: They stay fixed inside their own atoms
options.explanation: Fixed outer electrons would leave no electron sea, and the metallic bond would not exist.

check.stem: What is the metallic bond itself?

options.text: The strong attraction between the positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons
options.explanation: The bond names the electrostatic grip between the ion array and the shared electron sea.

options.text: The attraction between two positive ions
options.explanation: Two positive charges repel; the electrons between the ions are the joining party.

options.text: The attraction between delocalised electrons and each other
options.explanation: Like charges repel; the electrons bind to the positive ions, not to one another.

options.text: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
options.explanation: Shared pairs belong to covalent bonding; the metallic bond is collective, not pairwise.

check.stem: In a 2-D diagram of a metallic lattice, what must be shown?

options.text: Rows of positive ions with delocalised electrons distributed between them
options.explanation: The regular ion array and the free electrons between the rows are the two essential features.

options.text: Neutral atoms with all their electrons still attached
options.explanation: The lattice holds ions that have lost their outer electrons, not intact neutral atoms.

options.text: Alternating positive and negative ions
options.explanation: Alternating charges describe ionic lattices; a metal lattice is positive ions only, plus free electrons.

options.text: Molecules of metal joined by lines
options.explanation: Metals contain no molecules; the diagram shows the ion array and the electron sea.

check.stem: Where else does this type of bonding occur, besides pure metals?

options.text: In metal alloys, which are mixtures of metals
options.explanation: Alloys keep the same ion-plus-electron-sea structure, so the same bonding applies.

options.text: In ionic compounds dissolved in water
options.explanation: Dissolved ionic compounds conduct through moving ions, not through metallic bonding.

options.text: In giant covalent structures such as diamond
options.explanation: Diamond is a covalent network of non-metal atoms with no electron sea.

options.text: Nowhere else; only pure elements can bond metallically
options.explanation: Mixtures of metals share the same bonding, so alloys are included.

check.stem: Why are the delocalised electrons sometimes described as a sea?

options.text: Because they flow freely around and between all of the positive ions in the structure
options.explanation: The sea picture captures both the freedom of movement and the way every ion sits surrounded by the same electrons.

options.text: Because the electrons are wet and liquid
options.explanation: The sea is a model of movement, not a literal description of state.

options.text: Because they belong to one ion at a time
options.explanation: Belonging to one atom is exactly what delocalised electrons have given up.

options.text: Because they sit in fixed positions between the ions
options.explanation: Fixed positions contradict delocalisation; the sea flows.

lessons.title: Properties of metals
sourceHeadings: What are the properties of metals?
lessons.opening: The same bonding picture explains the typical physical properties of metals. Most metals have high melting and boiling points, because a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong attractions between the ions and the electron sea. Metals conduct electricity, because the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge. And most metals are malleable, because their layers of ions can slide over one another when a force is applied.
keyPoints: Most metals have high melting and boiling points, because strong electrostatic forces need lots of energy to break.
The forces grip between positively charged metal ions and the negatively charged electrons that surround them.
Metals conduct electricity because their delocalised electrons are available to move and carry charge.
Most metals are malleable, meaning they can be hammered into shape.
Malleability works because the atoms or ions form layers, and a push makes one layer slide across its neighbour.

low.restatement: Three properties, one cause. The grip between ions and the electron sea is strong, so melting takes high temperatures. The sea can flow, so metals conduct. And because the ion rows are neat layers, a hammer makes one layer slide past the next without breaking the grip, so the metal reshapes instead of shattering.
low.analogy: Think of a stack of identical trays in thick syrup: the syrup grips everything (high melting point), the syrup itself can flow (conduction), and one tray can slide sideways off its neighbour without tearing anything (malleability).
low.examPointer: The exam insists on correct terminology: for malleability, refer to atoms or ions in layers, never just particles, or the mark is lost.

medium.restatement: Each property maps onto the bonding model: high melting points follow from the strong electrostatic attraction between ions and the electron sea; conductivity follows from mobile delocalised electrons carrying charge through the lattice; and malleability follows from the regular layering of ions, which lets planes slide under force while the collective bond persists.
medium.analogy: Picture a deck of cards gripped loosely by a rubber band: the band holds the whole deck together, individual cards can still slide, and a coin dropped through the deck can drift from one end to the other.
medium.examPointer: Property questions are explanation questions: name the structural feature first, then attach the property, and keep the atoms-and-ions wording for malleability.

check.stem: Why do most metals have high melting and boiling points?

options.text: Strong electrostatic forces between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons need lots of energy to overcome
options.explanation: Melting must loosen the ion-electron grip throughout the giant lattice, and that grip is strong.

options.text: Metal atoms are very large and hard to move
options.explanation: Size is not the cause; the strength of the attractions between ions and electrons is.

options.text: The delocalised electrons hold their positions firmly
options.explanation: The electrons are mobile by definition; the melting point reflects the strong attraction, not electron fixation.

options.text: Melting requires breaking covalent bonds between metal atoms
options.explanation: Metals contain no covalent bonds; the forces are electrostatic between ions and the electron sea.

options.text: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice and carry the charge
options.explanation: The mobile electron sea is the charge carrier that lets a current flow through the metal.

options.text: The positive ions drift through the solid
options.explanation: The ions stay in their lattice positions; the electrons do the moving in a solid metal.

options.text: Metals are molten at room temperature
options.explanation: Metals are solid at room temperature and still conduct, which rules the state out as the cause.

options.text: Their layers slide, letting charge pass
options.explanation: Layer sliding explains malleability; conduction is the electron sea's work.

options.text: Their atoms or ions are arranged in layers that can slide over each other when a force is applied
options.explanation: Sliding layers let the metal change shape without fracturing, which is what malleable means.

options.text: Their bonds break easily and reform elsewhere
options.explanation: The bonding persists while layers slide; breaking and reforming is not the model used here.

options.text: The electron sea pushes the ions into new shapes
options.explanation: The sea maintains the bonding; reshaping follows from layer sliding under force.

options.text: Metals are soft because their ions carry high charges
options.explanation: Charge size affects melting point, not the layer-sliding that gives malleability.

check.stem: A student writes that metals are malleable because the particles can move. What is wrong with the wording?

options.text: The answer must refer to atoms or ions in layers sliding over each other, not just particles
options.explanation: The exam hint demands the correct terminology: layers of atoms or ions, sliding under force.

options.text: Nothing; particles is the preferred word
options.explanation: The generic word particles misses the structural point that the layers of ions are what slide.

options.text: The moving particles are the electrons, not the ions
options.explanation: Electron movement explains conduction; malleability is about the ion layers moving relative to each other.

options.text: Malleability should be explained by weak covalent bonds
options.explanation: No covalent bonds exist in a metal; the explanation is layer sliding within the metallic structure.

check.stem: Which property-equation pairing is correct for a typical metal?

options.text: Delocalised electrons give conduction, and layers of ions give malleability
options.explanation: Each property traces to its own structural feature: mobile electrons for conduction, sliding layers for malleability.

options.text: Delocalised electrons give malleability, and layers of ions give conduction
options.explanation: The two explanations have been swapped between the properties.

options.text: High melting points come from sliding layers
options.explanation: Sliding layers explain malleability; the melting point follows from the strong ion-electron attraction.

options.text: Conduction comes from ions moving between lattice sites
options.explanation: In a solid metal the ions are fixed; the electrons are the mobile carriers.

glossary.definition: Describing electrons that no longer belong to any specific atom and can move freely through the structure.
The strong attraction between positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons around them.
The regular, repeating arrangement of particles in a solid; in a metal, rows of positive ions.
Describing a material that can be hammered into shape because its layers can slide over each other.
A mixture of a metal with other elements, which keeps the metallic bonding of the parent structure.
